headline: A Jekyll theme grows into an AI-maintained site-building platform
summary: zer0-mistakes began in June 2024 as an imported Jekyll theme, then sat mostly idle for a year apart from small content edits and version bumps. From July 2025 it gained an installer, CI and a test suite, and through late 2025 and early 2026 it added analytics, Mermaid, Jupyter rendering, a feature registry and a large documentation set. Version 1.0.0 in April 2026 rewrote the installer and added admin dashboards and Obsidian support. From June 2026 most commits were AI-assisted or bot-made, working from a machine-readable backlog under a single-trunk release model. The project then expanded into translations, an embedded Claude/Grok Site Builder and a Rails studio app, and ended with a run of accessibility, performance and consent fixes.

eras.title: Theme Import and Long Dormancy
eras.summary: A burst of 33 commits in June 2024 imported the zer0 Jekyll theme with layouts, includes, assets, a sidebar and a long README. The following months saw only a handful of commits: blog edits, a README test commit, version bumps to 0.1.7 and 0.1.8, and a 404 page with a Docker compose file in March 2025.
eras.frontend: Visitors saw a Jekyll blog and landing page with a left sidebar, feature documentation pages and, from March 2025, a 404 page.
eras.backend: The work was mostly config and build changes around Gemfile, frontmatter.json and package.json, plus a first Docker compose file.
transitions: from an empty repository to a working Jekyll theme
from active setup to occasional maintenance edits

learnings.lesson: Commit Gemfile.lock and dependency choices deliberately at import time; removing hundreds of lock lines immediately afterwards suggests the dependency baseline was not settled.

eras.title: Installer, CI and Test Foundations
eras.summary: Development resumed with an install script, gem release workflows and Docker-first development, followed by remote installation and Azure Static Web Apps support. In September, 57 commits added test suites, performance and quality runners and a gem publish script. October brought a statistics dashboard (v0.4.0), a sitemap layout, Mermaid v2 and Copilot instruction files.
eras.frontend: Visitors began to see a Bootstrap statistics dashboard, a unified sitemap with search, and Mermaid diagrams.
eras.backend: The repository gained .github workflows, scripts/, test/ and lib/ directories, semantic-version publishing and AI-agent instruction files.
transitions: from a static theme to an installable gem with CI
from manual releases to scripted changelog and version bumps

learnings.lesson: Design CI workflows to be few and consolidated from the start; the September enhanced-CI workflow was deleted within the same month.
Agree on a test-suite taxonomy (core, deployment, quality) before adding runner scripts so that CI does not need rewiring later.

eras.title: Modular Scripts and Feature Sprawl
eras.summary: Large release and build scripts were split into modular shell libraries and then reorganised again into subdirectories, while five workflows became three. The site gained a blog redesign, Jupyter rendering, AI preview images, ES6 navigation and a features registry that grew from 3 to 43 entries. Documentation was split into user and developer sections, and in March 2026 frontend libraries were vendored for GitHub Pages.
eras.frontend: Visitors saw a redesigned blog with category and tag archives, notebook pages, hover-dropdown navigation, a feature showcase, a personalization page and, later, JSON-LD-backed FAQ and glossary pages.
eras.backend: Scripts were restructured twice (bin, utils, features and test, then thin wrappers), .devcontainer and templates were added, and Docker Hub publishing moved to GitHub variables.
transitions: from monolithic shell scripts to modular libraries
from scattered root docs to separated user and developer documentation
from CDN-loaded frontend libraries to vendored assets

learnings.lesson: Settle the scripts directory layout in one pass; restructuring in November and again in December required backward-compatibility wrappers.
Keep one feature registry from the beginning; expanding features.yml twice and later deleting a duplicate copy shows the cost of letting it drift.

eras.title: Road to 1.0 and Platform Features
eras.summary: The monolithic install.sh was replaced by a modular CLI with deploy targets and a test matrix, and version 1.0.0 shipped. Admin configuration dashboards, Obsidian vault support and frontmatter validation followed. In May, the team introduced design tokens, a second modular installer with an AI wizard, a leaner build without jQuery, and agent prompts compressed by about 70 percent.
eras.frontend: Visitors saw admin dashboards, Obsidian-style wiki links and backlinks, a sidebar rail, design-token styling and rewritten quickstart guides with a decision flowchart.
eras.backend: Bots began producing most commits; the installer became a plugin-based CLI, frontmatter got a schema linter, and MathJax loaded only when needed.
transitions: from a monolithic installer to a modular CLI with deploy plugins
from human-led commits to bot-heavy automation
from jQuery to a lighter build

learnings.lesson: Keep agent instruction files short from the start; compressing them by 70 percent later suggests the verbose versions were adding cost without value.
Add a test matrix before rewriting the installer, since the installer was rewritten twice in two months.

eras.title: AI-Driven Trunk and Governance
eras.summary: June 2026 had the busiest month on record, with 139 commits, 78 of them AI-assisted. A Year of AI content-hub pivot was reverted, the site briefly went offline before its domain was restored, and a single-trunk release model with CODEOWNERS and a machine-readable agent backlog was adopted. July consolidated preview-image engines, introduced AI-generated translations, reorganised the Playwright tests and replaced the feedback dropdown with a runtime issue widget.
eras.frontend: Visitors saw the theme landing page restored, a language toggle, better mobile overlays and a feedback widget that files GitHub issues.
eras.backend: The repository gained a backlog in .issues and .claude, a CSS diff harness for SCSS refactors, docs freshness checks and CI enforcement of one-paragraph-per-line prose.
transitions: from ad-hoc commits to a backlog-driven AI agent workflow
from hand-maintained translations to a build-time AI pipeline
from multiple release branches to a single trunk

learnings.lesson: Protect the CNAME and site identity with CI checks; a content pivot took zer0-mistakes.com offline and both changes had to be reverted.
Gate refactors with a visual or CSS diff harness, as was done for the SCSS restructure, so that large AI-made changes can be checked mechanically.

eras.title: Showcases and the Site Builder
eras.summary: The theme added demonstration content: a French locale, an examples directory, a cookbook collection, and design tokens aligned with the Claude Design system. September expanded the setup wizard into a nine-step Site Builder with embedded Claude and Grok sessions, made Mermaid diagrams accessible, and added a CI lane that produces visual evidence.
eras.frontend: Visitors could browse French pages, a cookbook with recipe scaling, an Obsidian-style graph view, view counts, and zoomable Mermaid figures, and could build a site through a chat-driven wizard.
eras.backend: New fr, examples and _design-system directories appeared, and three issue-URL builders were unified behind one shared feedback core.
transitions: from theme internals to showcase content and examples
from a static setup wizard to an LLM-backed Site Builder

learnings.lesson: Build shared cores before duplicating helpers; three separate issue-URL builders had to be merged after the feedback widget shipped.
Check that developer-only banners are excluded from rendered output before shipping docs, since they reached visitors.

eras.title: Studio App and Quality Hardening
eras.summary: A Rails 8.1 studio app was added for designing the theme in a browser. Most remaining work was fixes: performance (lazy sitemap rows, LCP image), consent-gated analytics, WCAG AA contrast, mobile admin layouts, and making newsletter and giscus integrations configurable for theme consumers.
eras.frontend: Visitors saw a simpler two-tier navbar, faster pages, no analytics before consent, higher-contrast skins and larger touch targets.
eras.backend: A studio/ Rails app was added, features.yml became a single registry, and a consumer audit script now detects stale vendored data.
transitions: from feature expansion to performance, privacy and accessibility fixes
from hard-coded integrations to consumer-configurable options

learnings.lesson: Load analytics only after consent from day one; PostHog and GA had been loading before consent until October 2026.
Make third-party integrations configurable when they are introduced; giscus and the newsletter form had to be retrofitted for consumers.
Fix the directory layout for scripts and installers once, with tests first; the installer and scripts were each restructured two or three times.
Keep a single source of truth for registries and config; duplicate features.yml files and hard-coded repo and Docker names both needed cleanup.
When AI agents produce most commits, add mechanical guards such as CODEOWNERS, CSS diff checks and visual baselines before expanding scope.
Guard the site identity and domain in CI; the content pivot that took the site offline cost a revert and a restore.
Treat privacy and accessibility as defaults rather than late fixes; consent-gated analytics and WCAG AA contrast arrived only after more than two years of development.

transitions.to: an installable gem with CI and release workflows
modular shell libraries and consolidated workflows
version 1.0.0 with a modular CLI installer
a backlog-driven, mostly AI-assisted single-trunk workflow
a Rails studio app plus performance, privacy and accessibility hardening
